sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: var m map[string]int is nil — reads work (zero values), WRITES panic. The fix: m = make(map[string]int) or a literal m := map[string]int{}. Every write needs the map initialized.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The panic, reproduced:

```go
var m map[string]int

// Reads work — nil map reads return zero values
v := m["key"]        // 0 — no error, no panic
_, ok := m["key"]    // (0, false) — safe

// WRITE panics
m["key"] = 1
// panic: assignment to entry in nil map
```

The root cause: a map value is a pointer to the hash-table structure. var m is nil — the pointer points at nothing. A read of 'nothing' honestly answers 'not there' (the zero value). A write to 'nothing' has nowhere to put the entry — the runtime refuses with a panic.

The fix — make the map:
```go
m := make(map[string]int)        // empty, write-ready
m := map[string]int{}            // literal — same, write-ready
m := map[string]int{"k": 1}     // with initial values
```

The classic causes:
1. Declared var m map[...]... and forgot the make
2. A struct with a map field not initialized in the constructor (the zero value struct has a nil map)
3. Passing a nil map into a function that populates it — the function can't fix the caller's nil (make inside doesn't reassign the caller's variable)

The fix pattern for the struct case: initialize in the constructor or immediately:
```go
type Cache struct {
    data map[string]string
}
func NewCache() *Cache {
    return &Cache{data: make(map[string]string)}  // NEVER nil
}
```

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    V[var m map] --> NIL[nil pointer]
    NIL --> R[m key: read → zero value — safe]
    NIL --> W[m key = 1 → PANIC: assignment to entry in nil map]
    MK[m := make] --> READY[write-ready]
    LIT[m := map literal] --> READY
    P[pass nil to populate fn] --> TRAP[made inside ≠ caller's map fixed]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the asymmetry with slices: a nil slice can be appended (append allocates the backing storage — the header IS the value). A nil map cannot be written — the map's structure (hash table, buckets, seeds) must be created by make; there's no 'lazily create on write' path because the map is already a pointer (the write would need to reassign the pointer, which Go's assignment semantics won't do through a map variable).

The function-parameter trap, expanded: populateMap(m map[string]int) with a nil m: making a NEW map inside the function creates a local — the caller's nil stays nil. The correct API: return the map (func makeMap() map[string]int), or take a *map, or (the Go-idiomatic form) the function makes and returns: callers compose.

The read-on-nil design rationale: 'total functions' — a read from any map (nil or empty) returns a value. The zero-value read lets accumulation code (m[k]++ — reads then writes) work on an EMPTY map, with the nil case being the single excluded state (the write panic is the deliberate loud failure).
